<reason>Both sides were sharp, adaptive, and grounded in plausible general knowledge without fake precision. CON's best work was structural: reframing consent as the "delivery mechanism," distinguishing recolonisation and federal-park cases from deliberate release, and the late function-vs-survival turn on Idaho. But CON's route to victory depended on two things it never repaired. First, it conceded in its opening that deer overpopulation is "a policy failure" fixable by culling "where governments fund them properly," and PRO converted that concession into a decisive question — what happens when the cheque is refused? CON's answer ("move, redesign, fund the cull properly in the meantime") is exactly the century-long status quo PRO indicted, and CON never explained why the political will it says is absent for wolves will materialise for deer. Second, CON's "consent is purchasable" [B2.7] handed PRO the mechanism and narrowed CON to the residual coercion case, where PRO held the cleaner comparison: predators plus grumbling versus no predators plus stripped hills. PRO also squarely met CON's hardest pressure question with the strongest available answer set (Idaho 1995 releases over state-legislature refusal, Mexican wolves on working rangeland, Jura/Slovenian lynx, Scottish sea eagles) and correctly exposed that CON's question ruled out every category of success in advance. CON's closing reframe — coercion buys the animal but loses the ecological function — is genuinely clever and does real damage, but it arrives late and was partly pre-empted by PRO's point that French and European populations kept rising under quotas and downlisting, and that no government has asked predators to leave. CON also slipped into arguing process rather than the motion's ecology when it accepted walked-in wolves. Both used the required A1:/A2: labels and asked genuine questions. PRO wins on the comparative that survived: some predators under management beats a conceded-failed cull regime.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's exploitation of CON's own concessions: pairing "deer numbers are a policy failure" [B1.6] with "consent is purchasable" [B2.7] to force the question "what happens when the cheque is refused?" CON's answer — redesign and "fund the cull properly in the meantime" — collapsed into the very status quo it had already admitted was broken. CON's counter-punch on Idaho's post-delisting cull [B4.5] was the sharpest reply of the debate, but PRO blunted it with "Idaho cut its wolves and still has hundreds," leaving the comparative intact.</best_rebuttal>
